newsitem.title: USA: US zinc physical market quiet amid LME volatility.
newsitem.headline: US zinc physical market quiet amid LME volatility.

text.p: The U.S. zinc physical market is eeriely quiet as most consumers lay low, waiting for the recent volatility to subside, dealers and producers said.
Zinc premiums have edged up slightly to 4.00-4.25 cents over LME cash, up 0.50-0.75 cent from last week's U.S. Mint tender, but down from the 4.75-6.00 cents the market saw a month ago.

"The galvanizers tend to lay low whenever the market gets this crazy," said one U.S. zinc producer. "They spent the last month waiting for a correction and they haven't seen one -- unless today counts."
Zinc prices have been rising steadily throughout 1997, but in the last month the LME three-month price has skyrocketed from $1,386 a tonne on June 27 to a high of $1,675 Monday.
Tuesday, the market erased all of the previous month's gains, but rebounded to $1,490 a tonne at the close of Tuesday's afternoon kerb.
The volatility is attrbuted to a squeeze of Chinese smelters who are believed to have been caught on the wrong side of a major short position.

In comparison, merchants report few bookings. "Most of my customers are holding off until they see where this thing ends up," said a Northeast merchant. "The market ran up too much too fast and now it's correcting with a vengence. Meanwhile, physical demand is rather lackluster."
The bulls in London have said that the sharp decline in London Metal Exchange warehouse stocks is the result of exports to the U.S., which is fueling worldwide demand.

"They're exporting to the U.S. at these premiums? It makes no sense," the merchant said, noting that the break-even premium level for export is 4.50-5.00 cents over LME cash. "More likely, there's a little red-lining going on," he said refering to the practice of removing metal from LME warrant without moving the metal from the warehouse.

Producers tended to be more bullish. "LME warehouse stocks have fallen more than 100,000 tonnes since the beginning of the year," said one U.S. producer. "You can't tell me that's all red-lining. Some of it had definitely come over to the U.S. May be not at these levels. But stocks have been falling all year.
"I agree that a lot of the zinc market now is fun and games," he added. "But we wouldn't be seeing this kind of volatility if there wasn't a genuinely strong market for zinc."
((Derek J. Caney, New York Commodity Desk, 212-859-1646))
